t5-game-theory: Game theory studies strategic interaction between rational decision-makers. Heads-up poker (ignoring rake) is a classic two-player zero-sum game: one side's gain is exactly the other's loss. Von Neumann's 1928 minimax theorem proves such games always have an "optimal strategy pair" — when both sides play their respective strategies, neither can profit by changing unilaterally.

Nash Equilibrium: a set of strategies where no single player can improve by deviating unilaterally. John Nash proved it exists in an extremely broad class of games — poker's GTO strategy is precisely poker's Nash equilibrium.

Zero-sum math: heads-up U₁(a,b) + U₂(a,b) = 0 (one side's gain is the other's loss)
Minimax theorem: there exists a game value v such that max_a min_b U₁(a,b) = min_b max_a U₁(a,b) = v
An equilibrium strategy guarantees your expectation ≥ v, and the opponent can't unilaterally push it lower — this is the mathematical source of being "unexploitable" (concept from: The Mathematics of Poker Ch.2 basic game theory)
What Equilibrium Means — and Common Misreadings

The equilibrium strategy is "unexploitable": no matter how the opponent plays, your expectation is never below the game value. It doesn't promise to "win the most" — against a maniac donating money, the equilibrium strategy earns less than a targeted exploitative one. Equilibrium is the floor, exploitation is the ceiling; this tension runs through all advanced theory (unified in T9).

Example: Rock-paper-scissors' equilibrium is randomizing each 1/3. If the opponent always throws rock, the equilibrium strategy still breaks even (expectation 0), but the exploitative "always paper" wins every round. However, if you always throw paper you become exploitable yourself (he switches to scissors) — deviating from equilibrium to exploit necessarily opens your own leaks. Poker is exactly isomorphic.

Example 2 (minimax in a toy game): You write 1 or 2, the opponent guesses; if he guesses right you lose 1, if wrong you win 2. When you mix 50/50, his expectation guessing 1 = 0.5×1 + 0.5×(−2) = −0.5, and guessing 2 = 0.5×(−2) + 0.5×1 = −0.5 — both sides equal, so you lock in +0.5. Any deviation lets him pick the favorable side and push your expectation down. Poker solvers do exactly the same thing: at each node find the mixing ratio that makes all opponent responses indifferent.

If your strategy is deterministic (same spot, same action forever), observant opponents will eventually decipher and counter it. An equilibrium strategy therefore must include mixed components: the same hand at the same node splits across actions by certain probabilities (detailed in this level's "Mixed Strategies, Indifference & Node Locking" chapter). Randomizing isn't indecisiveness — it's a mathematical weapon that makes any opponent guess unprofitable.

Important multiway warning: the Nash "unexploitable" guarantee strictly holds only for two-player zero-sum games. In pots with three or more, even if everyone plays "equilibrium", coalition effects can damage one side. Theoretical tools all have applicability boundaries. How multiway frequencies and sizings are recomputed appears in this level's “Multiway Pot Frequencies and Sizings” chapter; the full discussion of why the equilibrium guarantee fails is in T9 “Multiway Pot Theory”.

Think of equilibrium as a "bulletproof vest", not a "weapon": wear it against strong and unknown opponents for safety, take it off and switch to a knife (exploitation) once you identify weaknesses — knowing when to wear it and when to take it off is the real skill.
t5-gto-concept: GTO (Game Theoretically Optimal) refers to poker's Nash equilibrium strategy. Solvers approximate it through massive iteration: given preflop ranges, stack depth, and available sizings, they output each hand's action frequency at every node. GTO is the "origin of the coordinate system" for strategy — not an answer to copy verbatim, but the benchmark for measuring every deviation.

Intuitive features of GTO: every bet is composed of value and bluffs in a specific ratio; every calling range makes the opponent's bluffs exactly break even; every sizing choice makes all opponent responses indifferent. It is "exactly right" everywhere — no more, no less.

Value:bluff ratio derivation (pot P, bet bP, opponent has a bluff catcher):
Opponent call EV = f×(P+bP) − (1−f)×bP, set = 0 (indifferent) → f = b/(1+2b) (f = your bluff share of the betting range)
Example: full pot b=1 → bluffs 1/3 (value:bluff = 2:1); half pot b=0.5 → bluffs 25% (3:1) (concept from: Modern Poker Theory Ch.2-3 GTO structure)

This ratio exactly equals the pot odds the opponent needs to call — making his call and fold EV with a bluff catcher identical (indifferent). The bigger the bet, the more bluffs it can carry: the mathematical root of "big size = polarization" (detailed in T6). On the turn and flop, because more streets remain, bluff share can be higher (some bluffs later give up or convert).

Example: On the river you full-pot bet; your range should be about 2/3 value + 1/3 bluffs. If you actually "only bet nuts" (0% bluffs), the opponent can exploit you by folding everything to your bets; if you bluff more than half, he exploits you by calling everything. The equilibrium ratio is the only construction that leaves the opponent helpless either way.

Example 2 (minimum necessary deviation): You observe an opponent who only calls big river bets 30% of the time (equilibrium ~50%). Based on this you can raise your river overbet bluff frequency overall — but cap the adjustment at "I still don't lose if he corrects to 40%", keeping room to return to baseline anytime. This is exactly the executable example of "using GTO as baseline, making directed, disciplined deviations from observable biases".
The Correct Relationship Between GTO and Exploitation

The mature framework in practice: use GTO as the baseline to understand what each node "should" look like, then make minimal necessary deviations based on the opponent's observable biases (Maximally Exploitative in direction, Minimally Exploitative in magnitude). The baseline gives you invincibility; the deviations give you profit. Exploitation without GTO is running naked; GTO without deviation is self-shackling.

Common misreading: "GTO is playing tight" or "GTO is balancing to the point of boredom". In fact solver strategies are full of high-frequency bluffs, overbet shoves, and thin value — it just keeps all of it at ratios the opponent can't counter.

When studying solver outputs, don't memorize frequencies; ask three whys: why this sizing on this board? Why does this hand go into the betting range and that one into the checking range? Why did the frequency change on the turn? Understand the structure and the frequencies will remember themselves.
t5-mdf-alpha: MDF answers: facing a bet, what minimum share of my range must I continue with (call or raise) so the opponent's "any-two-card bluff" is unprofitable? If your defense is below MDF, the opponent needs no hand strength at all — every bet itself is a money printer.

MDF derivation (P = pot, B = bet, b = B/P, f = your fold rate):
Opponent pure-bluff EV = f×P − (1−f)×B, set = 0 → f = B/(P+B) = b/(1+b)
Your minimum defense frequency MDF = 1 − f = P/(P+B) = 1/(1+b)
Example: half pot b=0.5 → 67%; full pot b=1 → 50%; 2x pot b=2 → 33% (concept from: The Mathematics of Poker Ch.5-6 bet-fold subgame)
Alpha: The Bluff's Break-Even Fold Rate

Alpha (α) = bet ÷ (pot + bet) = b/(1+b) = 1 − MDF
Example: a half-pot bluff needs the opponent to fold ≥33% to break even; full pot needs ≥50%

MDF and Alpha are two sides of the same coin: when the defender's fold rate exactly equals α, the attacker's pure-bluff EV is zero — neither side can profit by changing frequency, which is the equilibrium point of this "bet-fold" subgame.

Example: Pot 100, opponent bets 50. MDF = 100/150 ≈ 67%, so you need to continue with roughly your strongest 67%. Choose which hands to continue by ranking hand strength + improvement potential: made hands and good draws first, pure garbage goes into the folding 33%. If you actually only defend 40%, the opponent instantly profits 0.60×100 − 0.40×50 = 40 on every 50 bluff.

Example 2 (overbets and MDF): Pot 100, opponent shoves 200 (b=2). MDF = 100/300 ≈ 33%, greatly reducing your defense burden; meanwhile the overbet's equilibrium bluff share b/(1+2b) = 2/5 = 40%, i.e. his range should be 60% value + 40% bluffs. Judging whether his "value:bluff" matches 3:2 matters more than mechanically memorizing MDF: if he's actually 90% value, your defense should drop below 33% — this is the correct combination of MDF and exploitation.

Defense isn't only calling: raises also count toward defense frequency. Against high-frequency bluffers, substitute some calls with raises to both defend and collect value; against tight-passive value bettors, over-folding (below MDF) is the exploitation. First compute the total, then allocate.

MDF is the floor against "balanced bluffing opponents", not a universal prescription: (1) against opponents who almost never bluff (many low-stakes players' big river bets), folding well below MDF is actually optimal exploitation; (2) in multiway pots the defense burden is shared (each player’s obligation = 1 − α^(1/n); see this level's “Multiway Pot Frequencies and Sizings” chapter) — not everyone needs to hit MDF; (3) with a raise option, defense can be built from calls plus raises. Remember: equilibrium frequencies are the bulletproof vest when you lack opponent information; exploit first when you have information.
Memorize three practical anchors: defend 75% vs 1/3-pot bets, 67% vs half-pot, 50% vs full-pot. Whatever sits below the anchor is automatic profit you're handing the opponent.

The easiest leak to self-audit in review: track your actual fold rate against big turn/river bets. The vast majority of players fold far above equilibrium — which is why the opponent's big bets always seem to "just happen" to make you fold.

MDF, Alpha and required call equity side by side (b = bet as a multiple of the pot): MDF + Alpha = 100%, two sides of one coin; required call equity is always lower than Alpha because a call also wins the opponent's bet.
t5-mixed-strategy: Mixed Strategies and the Indifference Principle

Open any solver and you'll see: the same hand at the same node is often split across multiple actions (e.g. 70% bet / 30% check). The foundation is the Indifference Principle: in equilibrium, a hand is mixed only when all its actions have exactly equal EV; and the purpose of that mixing is to make the "opponent's" marginal hands (like bluff catchers) also exactly indifferent between calling and folding.

Indifference principle proof sketch (mixed hand H):
Let H's bet EV = V_b and check EV = V_c. If V_b > V_c, a rational strategy bets 100%; if V_b < V_c, it checks 100%
→ Mixing exists ⇔ V_b = V_c (by contradiction: any imbalance gets exploited by the opponent)
Similarly, the opponent's bluff catcher is indifferent between call/fold in equilibrium — the two indifferences jointly lock in the frequencies (concept from: Modern Poker Theory Ch.3 mixed strategies and indifference)

Division of labor between two hand types: "pure-strategy hands" in the range (unique clearly-best action, e.g. betting nuts, folding garbage) contribute most of the EV; "mixed hands" sit at the tipping point, and their frequency allocation is the glue that keeps the whole system unexploitable.

Example: On the river you hold a bluff catcher facing a full-pot bet. In equilibrium the opponent bluffs 1/3, and your required equity is exactly 33% — call and fold have identical EV. The solver might output something like "call 50% / fold 50%". Practical meaning: the single-decision cost of getting these wrong is ≈0, so don't agonize; the real EV differences hide in range construction on earlier streets.
How to Execute Mixing in Practice

Humans can't be truly random; use external random sources (watch the second hand, use dealt suit) or "simplify to pure strategies": split the mixed frequency by readable features (suited hands bet, offsuit check). For most players the more pragmatic path is: accept that choosing either side at a mixed node costs almost nothing, and invest practice time in decision points with high EV differences.
Node Locking: The Bridge From Equilibrium to Exploitation

Node locking is an advanced solver feature: "lock" the opponent's strategy at a node to the real tendency you observed (e.g. "this opponent never bluffs the river" or "folds to C-Bets 60%"), then re-solve your optimal response. The output is the maximally exploitative strategy against that leak.

Example: After locking "BB folds to turn double-barrel 55% (equilibrium ~45%)" and re-solving, the solver immediately pushes your turn bluff frequency higher, even adding weak hands that originally checked into the betting range — it precisely shows "how much you should deviate for every 1% the opponent deviates" to harvest. Node locking turns exploitation from intuition into calculation.

Example 2 (five-step node-locking workflow): ① collect enough HUD samples to confirm the leak (e.g. "BTN folds to 3-bet 65%"); ② lock that node to a fixed frequency in the solver; ③ re-solve your response and compare to baseline; ④ mark the specific hands whose frequencies and sizings got pushed up; ⑤ execute in play, re-checking the sample roughly every 500 hands to see if it still holds. A "lock" without data support is just exploitation on paper.

Node-locking discipline: the locked tendency must come from real observation over a sufficient sample, not single-hand impressions. Using imagined leaks for maximum exploitation is like swapping a bulletproof vest for a paper shirt.

Learning path suggestion: first use solvers to understand equilibrium shapes (the why), then use node locking to study "standard harvest schemes for common opponent leaks", finally validate in live play — close the three-step loop and theory becomes profit.
t5-multiway-frequency: More Defenders Means More Independent Checkpoints

The α and MDF in this level's “MDF & Alpha: Critical Frequencies of Defense and Attack” chapter rest on an implicit premise: exactly one opponent has not decided yet. As soon as two players are still to act after the flop, your bluff faces two separate "should I stop this" judgements. The defenders need no coordination — if either one is willing to call, your bluff fails. That turns the clean break-even line from heads-up play into a product problem.

All-fold probability is the product of the defenders’ fold rates, not their average: with n players still to act each folding at rate f, all-fold = fⁿ. Every extra defender raises f to one more power.

Conventions identical to this level's “MDF & Alpha: Critical Frequencies of Defense and Attack” chapter: P = pot before the bet, b = bet size, α = b ÷ (P + b), MDF = P ÷ (P + b).

Baseline (heads-up): pot 100, bet 50 (half pot) → α = 50 ÷ 150 = 33.3%, MDF = 100 ÷ 150 = 66.7%.
Meaning: the opponent folding 33.3% of the time already makes any two cards break even for you; defending 66.7% makes bluffing worthless.

With n players still to act, each defending at the heads-up MDF (fold rate 33.3%):
all-fold = 0.333² = 11.1% (two defenders)
all-fold = 0.333³ = 3.7% (three defenders)
(Concepts from: The Mathematics of Poker Ch.5 the bet-fold subgame; Multiway Theory equity distribution in multiway pots)
EV Collapse: What a Half-Pot Bluff Into Two Players Is Actually Worth

Bluff EV = all-fold rate × current pot − (1 − all-fold rate) × bet size. With P=100, b=50 and each defender folding 1/3:

1 defender: 0.333 × 100 − 0.667 × 50 = 33.3 − 33.3 = 0 (break-even, exactly the definition of α)
2 defenders: 0.111 × 100 − 0.889 × 50 = 11.1 − 44.4 = −33.3
3 defenders: 0.037 × 100 − 0.963 × 50 = 3.7 − 48.1 = −44.4

Now test "does a bigger sizing rescue it": switch to a pot-sized bet b=100, so α = 100 ÷ 200 = 50%, and two defenders each fold 50%:
all-fold = 0.5² = 25%, EV = 0.25 × 100 − 0.75 × 100 = −50
Conclusion: raising the sizing does not rescue the bluff — it scales the loss when called at the same time. Bluffs into multiway pots are not fixed by playing more aggressively.

Example 1 (a turn bluff with no showdown value): BTN opens, CO calls, and you defend in the BB with A♣8♣. Flop Q♥7♦2♠, turn 4♥, pot 100; CO and BTN are both still to act. You bet 50 as a pure bluff (ace-high, no pair, no draw). The heads-up instinct "bet 50 and I need him to fold a third of the time" fails completely here: if both defend at the MDF from this level's “MDF & Alpha: Critical Frequencies of Defense and Attack” chapter, your all-fold rate is only 11.1% and each attempt is −33.3bb. The correct action is not to bet bigger but to admit this hand has no bluffing licence in a multiway pot — check or fold, and keep the bluff budget for single-opponent spots.
Diffusion of Responsibility: How Each Defender’s Obligation Is Recomputed

Look at it from the other side: the bluffing player must clear two checkpoints, which is good news for the defenders — the two can free-ride on each other. If the other player is willing to stop the bluff, you do not have to. So each individual’s minimum defending frequency drops well below the heads-up MDF. But the drop is not "divide by the number of players", because the condition is not an allocation of quotas — it is the multiplicative requirement that at least one defender stops it often enough.

Let each defender call/defend with frequency d; then all-fold = (1 − d)ⁿ. Set it equal to the heads-up break-even fold rate α:
(1 − d)ⁿ = α → d = 1 − α^(1/n)

Half pot into a pot of 100: α = 1/3
Two defenders: d = 1 − (1/3)^(1/2) = 1 − 0.577 = 42.3% (heads-up was 66.7%)
Three defenders: d = 1 − (1/3)^(1/3) = 1 − 0.693 = 30.7%

Identity check: 1 − (1 − 0.423)² = 1 − 0.333 = 66.7% = the heads-up MDF.
That is the whole mechanism: each person defends less, yet the probability that at least one of them stops you is unchanged.
The common miscount: 66.7% ÷ 2 = 33.4%, nine points below the true obligation — a gap opponents collect directly by bluffing into you multiply.
(Concepts from: Multiway Theory diffusion of responsibility in multiway pots; Applications of No-Limit Hold’em multiway defending frequencies)

Example 2 (BB’s defending arithmetic facing a half-pot bet): BTN opens, CO calls, and you defend in the BB with A♦6♦. Flop 9♠7♠2♥: BB checks, CO checks, BTN bets 50 into 100. CO has already checked but is still behind you and can continue with a call or raise. Heads-up you would need roughly 66.7% defending to stop BTN bluffing any two cards; with CO also in the defensive chain, your personal obligation falls to 42.3%. Reasonable inference: CO’s range contains plenty of flushes and 9/7 type hands, so the "stopping" job is likely done by him, and you can fold this hand — that is not timidity but the optimal division of labour under a product structure. What is wrong is halving the obligation again to 33.4%: then you and CO both under-defend and BTN’s any two cards print.

Example 3 (the opposite conclusion for the value bettor): on the same board you are in the BB holding A♦Q♦ (top pair, top kicker); you bet 50 into 100 with CO and BTN still to act. The bluffer’s all-fold rate is crushed to 11.1% by the exponent, but a value bet wants the opposite event: with both defenders continuing at the heads-up MDF (each folding 1/3), at least one continues 1 − (1/3)² = 88.9% of the time — above the 66.7% heads-up continuation rate. So the same product law yields two disciplines: in multiway pots value bets are worth making and worth making thick, while pure bluffs fall out. Add the protection dimension: with two opponents holding four cards between them, approximating nine flush outs, the chance that at least one of them improves on the next card is roughly 1 − (1 − 9/47)² ≈ 35% (an illustrative estimate that treats opponent hands as random; the real number shifts with range), so the cost of slow-playing a free card rises with the number of live hands.

Two common ways to think wrong. First: "in multiway pots the opponents eliminate each other, so I can bluff more often" — that treats "the defenders may stop each other" as "the number of defenders is unchanged", while in reality your bluff must pass n checkpoints and the all-fold rate is squeezed by the exponent; and the callers in multiway pots have stronger continuing ranges, so the effective α is harder than the 1/n power already suggests. Second: "with more defenders my own obligation divides by the number of players" — the requirement is the product condition "at least one of us stops it", and dividing under-defends systematically (66.7% ÷ 2 = 33.4% versus the correct 42.3%). Both errors come from the same source: reading a multiplicative relation as a linear one.

Three questions before and after you enter the pot: ① How many players still have not decided on this street? Write down n and estimate all-fold as fⁿ. ② Is my range section bluffing or collecting value? The first loses value fast with n, the second gains. ③ If I am the defender, my obligation is 1 − α^(1/n), not MDF ÷ n. All three are mental arithmetic — the table does not need a solver.
Division of labour with T9: frequencies are computed here, discipline is set there

This chapter covers only the recomputation of frequencies and sizings: the product law for all-fold rates, the diffusion of defending responsibility, and the value/bluff asymmetry. The dilution of equity itself (AA falling from about 85% heads-up to about 64% four-way), the first law ("hands that can make the nuts gain value, easily dominated hands lose it"), and the full multiway discipline list are developed in T9 “Multiway Pot Theory”; the equity-realization layer is in T6 “Board Texture and Equity Realization”. All three use the same product structure, on different objects.

All-fold rate is the product of the defenders’ fold rates: a half pot into two players leaves 11.1%, into three leaves 3.7%
Bluff EV collapses with headcount (0 → −33.3 → −44.4), and bigger sizings make it worse (pot-sized into two: −50)
Defending obligations diffuse as d = 1 − α^(1/n): 42.3% each with two defenders, 30.7% with three; dividing MDF by headcount (33.4%) is systematic under-defence
Value and bluffs are asymmetric: with more players the chance that at least one calls goes up, so value gets thicker while pure bluffs leave the pot

t5-game-theory-q1.question: The definition of a Nash equilibrium is:
options: The strategy profile that maximizes everyone's payoff
A strategy profile where no single player benefits from deviating unilaterally
A strategy with over 50% win rate
t5-game-theory-q1.explanation: Equilibrium doesn't promise maximum payoff — only that "unilateral deviation is unprofitable", which is exactly where being unexploitable comes from.

t5-game-theory-q2.question: Against a leaky weak opponent, the equilibrium (GTO) strategy:
options: Doesn't lose, but earns less than targeted exploitation
Is identical to the exploitative strategy
t5-game-theory-q2.explanation: Equilibrium guarantees expectation no lower than the game value (a floor) but doesn't actively exploit opponent errors; exploitation extracts more — at the cost of opening your own leaks.

t5-game-theory-q3.question: An equilibrium strategy must include randomized (mixed) components because:
options: It makes the game more exciting
Deterministic strategies get observed and countered; mixing makes every opponent guess unprofitable
t5-game-theory-q3.explanation: A strategy that always takes the same action in the same spot can be deciphered. Mixing makes the opponent's expectation identical no matter which side he bets on — nothing to attack.

t5-game-theory-q4.question: The "unexploitable" guarantee of Nash equilibrium strictly applies to:
options: Pots of any size in player count
t5-game-theory-q4.explanation: In games with three or more players the equilibrium floor can fail (coalition dynamics can harm one side). Heads-up and "two players left preflop" are the strict applicability domain.

t5-game-theory-q5.question: In the toy game, mixing "write 1 / write 2" at 50/50 achieves:
options: The same expectation for the opponent on either guess, locking your payoff to the game value
t5-game-theory-q5.explanation: Once mixing makes all opponent choices equal in expectation, he can no longer push your payoff down — the minimax-locked game value. Poker solver mixing frequencies work the same way.

t5-gto-concept-q1.question: The equilibrium value:bluff ratio for a full-pot river bet is about:
t5-gto-concept-q1.explanation: Bluff share = b/(1+2b) = 1/3, i.e. 2/3 value and 1/3 bluffs, value:bluff = 2:1. It exactly equals the opponent's required call equity of 33%.

t5-gto-concept-q2.question: Why does a larger bet size allow the equilibrium strategy to carry more bluffs?
options: The opponent's required call equity rises, so the indifferent bluff share rises with it
Big bets can afford to lose
That's wrong — bluffs should be small
t5-gto-concept-q2.explanation: b/(1+2b) rises monotonically with b: the bigger the sizing, the worse the opponent's calling price, so your range can carry higher bluff density while keeping him indifferent.

t5-gto-concept-q3.question: The exploitable flaw in "you only bet the nuts big and never bluff" is:
options: The opponent can fold everything to your big bets
The opponent can call everything to your big bets
The opponent will re-raise you every time
t5-gto-concept-q3.explanation: A betting range with no bluffs means the opponent loses nothing by folding everything except the nuts — your value bets never get called and your strong hands' EV shrinks drastically.

t5-gto-concept-q4.question: The mature relationship between GTO and exploitation in practice is:
options: Pick one, it's a style choice
Use GTO as the baseline, deviate with direction based on observable opponent biases
GTO at low stakes, exploitation at high stakes
t5-gto-concept-q4.explanation: The baseline provides an unexploitable floor and the cognition of the "correct shape"; exploitation turns opponent errors into extra profit on top — they're foundation and floors of a building.

t5-gto-concept-q5.question: The equilibrium bluff share of a half-pot bet (formula f = b/(1+2b)) is:
t5-gto-concept-q5.explanation: b=0.5 → f = 0.5/2 = 25%, value:bluff = 3:1. It exactly equals the opponent's required call equity, making both sides indifferent.

t5-mdf-alpha-q1.question: Facing a half-pot bet, MDF is about:
t5-mdf-alpha-q1.explanation: MDF = 1/(1+0.5) = 2/3 ≈ 67%. You need to continue with roughly your strongest two-thirds, or any opponent bluff becomes profitable.

t5-mdf-alpha-q2.question: Alpha (α) represents:
options: The minimum frequency of value bets
The minimum fold rate a pure bluff needs to break even
The minimum equity needed to call
t5-mdf-alpha-q2.explanation: α = b/(1+b), the bluff's break-even fold rate, complementary to MDF (α = 1−MDF).

t5-mdf-alpha-q3.question: You only defend 30% against full-pot bets (MDF should be 50%). The opponent's correct exploitation is:
options: Raise bluff frequency with any two cards
t5-mdf-alpha-q3.explanation: A 70% fold rate far exceeds the 50% a full-pot bluff needs to break even — the opponent's bets with any two cards are automatically profitable, so he should bluff aggressively more.

t5-mdf-alpha-q4.question: When is folding well below MDF actually correct?
options: When you read the opponent as almost never bluffing
When the pot is especially big
t5-mdf-alpha-q4.explanation: MDF is the floor against balanced opponents. When his betting range is heavily value-skewed, over-folding is exactly maximizing exploitation — with information, exploitation beats equilibrium.

t5-mdf-alpha-q5.question: Pot 100, opponent bets 200 (2x pot). MDF is about:
t5-mdf-alpha-q5.explanation: MDF = 1/(1+2) = 1/3 ≈ 33%. Bigger bets shrink defense responsibility; but the overbet range's equilibrium bluff share rises to 40%, so judge by "value:bluff" matching rather than mechanically applying the defense floor.

t5-mixed-strategy-q1.question: In equilibrium, a hand is mixed across multiple actions only if:
options: The hand is too hard to decide
All actions have exactly equal EV
It was chosen randomly to confuse the opponent
t5-mixed-strategy-q1.explanation: Indifference principle: when EV differs, a rational strategy always picks the higher one. Mixing only occurs on critical hands with equal EV, and its frequencies maintain the opponent's indifference.

t5-mixed-strategy-q2.question: Against an equilibrium opponent's full-pot bet, your bluff catcher's call and fold EV are:
t5-mixed-strategy-q2.explanation: The equilibrium bluff share makes your equity exactly equal the required equity — the two actions are indifferent. That's how equilibrium "leaves the opponent torn".

t5-mixed-strategy-q3.question: The purpose of node locking is:
options: Lock your own strategy to prevent misclicks
Fix the opponent's strategy to the observed real tendency and solve the maximally exploitative response
t5-mixed-strategy-q3.explanation: Node locking feeds "how the opponent actually plays" into the solver and outputs the optimal harvest scheme for that deviation — the bridge from equilibrium tools to exploitation.

t5-mixed-strategy-q4.question: For live players, the most pragmatic attitude toward mixed-strategy nodes is:
options: Recognize that either side loses almost nothing, and invest effort in high-EV-difference decisions
Avoid all spots where mixing appears
t5-mixed-strategy-q4.explanation: Both sides of a mixed node have equal EV, so a single "wrong choice" costs ≈0; what actually separates results is pure-strategy nodes and range construction on earlier streets.

t5-mixed-strategy-q5.question: The most critical execution discipline in node locking is:
options: Set the locked frequency as high as possible
The locked opponent tendency must come from real observation over a sufficient sample, and be re-checked periodically
A lock lasts forever once set
Locks can only be used on preflop ranges
t5-mixed-strategy-q5.explanation: Locking imaginary leaks into the solver produces "exploitation on paper"; real biases need HUD sample support and re-verification as the opponent adjusts — that's the line between node locking and self-deception.

t5-multiway-frequency-q1.question: Pot 100, you bet 50 (half pot) and two players still to act each defend at the heads-up MDF. Your all-fold rate is about:
t5-multiway-frequency-q1.explanation: Each defender’s fold rate is α = 1/3, so two of them give (1/3)² = 11.1%. 33% is the heads-up case; 25% is the pot-sized bet into two defenders folding 50% each; 3.7% is three defenders. All four figures appear in the text — the confusion comes from treating headcount as an additive condition.

t5-multiway-frequency-q2.question: Does increasing the sizing from half pot to pot size make bluffing into a multiway pot profitable again?
options: Yes — the bigger the bet, the higher the fold rate
No: pot-sized into two defenders folding 50% each gives 25% all-fold while doubling the loss when called, so EV gets worse
No, because pot odds dilute as players are added
Yes, provided one of the opponents is tight
t5-multiway-frequency-q2.explanation: EV = 0.25×100 − 0.75×100 = −50, worse than the −33.3 of a half pot into two: a larger sizing raises both the loss when called and the defenders’ fold rate, while all-fold stays under multiplicative pressure. Option one ignores that defending frequency rises with size; option three makes the odds offered to callers the deciding factor, but profit depends on the ratio of all-fold rate to risk; option four turns "one opponent happens to be tight" into something sizing can fix.

t5-multiway-frequency-q3.question: Facing a half-pot bet with two defenders, roughly what is each one’s minimum defending frequency?
t5-multiway-frequency-q3.explanation: d = 1 − α^(1/2) = 1 − (1/3)^(1/2) = 42.3%. 33.4% is precisely the common "66.7% ÷ 2" miscount; 66.7% is the heads-up obligation (everyone defending that much would leave the bluffer no hope); 37.5% is an unsourced intermediate value.

t5-multiway-frequency-q4.question: Why does "each person defends less, yet at least one of them stops the bluff just as often" hold?
options: Because defenders can agree out loud to take turns
Because 1 − (1 − d)ⁿ returns exactly to the heads-up MDF — the requirement itself is multiplicative
Because the pot grows with headcount, so each player can invest less
Because bluffs are simply rare in multiway pots
t5-multiway-frequency-q4.explanation: The identity 1 − (1 − 0.423)² = 66.7% is the entire mechanism. Option one mistook a structural diffusion for collusion; option three conflates pot size with a frequency obligation; option four states a consequence as if it were the cause — it is precisely because bluffing becomes unprofitable that the defending obligation falls.

t5-multiway-frequency-q5.question: For a value bet, the same product law means:
options: Value bets should also decrease with headcount, since the pot is harder to win
Value bets are worth making more often: the chance at least one player continues (88.9% with two defenders each defending at the heads-up MDF) exceeds the 66.7% heads-up rate
Value bets should be converted into checks so opponents act first
Exactly as with bluffs: value decays exponentially with headcount
t5-multiway-frequency-q5.explanation: A bluff needs "everyone folds" (squeezed by the exponent: 11.1%) while a value bet needs "at least one continues" (pushed up by it: 1 − (1/3)² = 88.9%) — two sides of the same expression. Options one and four confuse the two sides, ignoring that being called is a gain for a value bet; option three voluntarily gives up the higher continuation probability a multiway pot offers, i.e. it plays a value hand like a bluff.

t5-game-theory-q6.question: A Nash equilibrium strategy guarantees:
options: no unilateral deviation helps, an unexploitable floor
t5-game-theory-q6.explanation: Equilibrium promises no profitable unilateral deviation, not maximum profit. Exploitative play may earn more against specific opponents but gives up this floor.

t5-game-theory-q7.question: Poker strategy must include randomness (mixing) because:
options: deterministic strategies get decoded and exploited
t5-game-theory-q7.explanation: A fixed strategy is readable and counterable over enough samples; frequency mixing prevents opponents from inferring holdings and preserves unexploitability.

t5-game-theory-q8.question: When does the unexploitability guarantee of Nash equilibrium fail?
options: multiway pots with three or more players
t5-game-theory-q8.explanation: The strict guarantee rests on two-player zero-sum games; in a three-way pot even equilibrium play can create coalition effects that hurt one player. Every tool has a boundary.

t5-gto-concept-q6.question: The equilibrium value-to-bluff ratio for a pot-size bet is about:
t5-gto-concept-q6.explanation: At pot size the bluff share is y = b/(1+2b) = 1/3, so value to bluff is 2:1. Larger sizes permit a higher bluff share.

t5-gto-concept-q7.question: The correct role of GTO in practice is:
options: a baseline for measuring deviations, not a script to copy
the only correct play, any deviation is a mistake
t5-gto-concept-q7.explanation: GTO supplies an unexploitable baseline that tells you the direction and size of deviations; against clear leaks, copying equilibrium is often not maximum EV.

t5-gto-concept-q8.question: How is an opponent who only bets the nuts and never bluffs exploited?
options: opponents fold everything non-nut, so value bets earn no calls
t5-gto-concept-q8.explanation: A betting range without bluffs can be answered by folding everything, so value hands only win folds. Value and bluffs must stay proportional for a range to be unexploitable.

t5-mdf-alpha-q6.question: Facing a one-third pot bet, the minimum defense frequency is about:
t5-mdf-alpha-q6.explanation: MDF = 1 ÷ (1+b); with b=1/3 it is 1 ÷ (4/3) = 75%. Alpha for one-third pot is 25%, the complement.

t5-mdf-alpha-q7.question: Alpha (the break-even fold rate for a bluff) at one-third pot is:
t5-mdf-alpha-q7.explanation: Alpha = b ÷ (1+b) = (1/3) ÷ (4/3) = 25%. 20% is the caller's required equity, not the aggressor's needed fold rate.

t5-mdf-alpha-q8.question: Against a tight, value-only opponent who almost never bluffs, the correct defense frequency is:
options: MDF applies only on the river
t5-mdf-alpha-q8.explanation: MDF assumes the opponent bluffs with any two cards. Against almost no bluffs, over-folding is the exploit; defending at MDF donates to their value range.

t5-mixed-strategy-q6.question: A hand is mixed across actions exactly when:
t5-mixed-strategy-q6.explanation: The indifference principle: only equal EVs make any frequency mix EV-neutral while hiding your hand. When EVs differ, play the highest-EV action purely.

t5-mixed-strategy-q7.question: Node-locking for maximum exploit requires:
options: a stable tendency supported by enough samples
t5-mixed-strategy-q7.explanation: Node locking fixes an observed bias in the solver. Exploiting a one-hand impression trades armor for paper; without sample size the bias may be noise.

t5-mixed-strategy-q8.question: The main function of mixed strategy in an equilibrium system is to:
options: hide your hand and stay unexploitable
t5-mixed-strategy-q8.explanation: Mixed hands sit at indifference points; their frequency split is the glue of unexploitability. The result of any single mix is irrelevant.

t5-multiway-frequency-q6.question: A half-pot bluff faces two defenders who each fold one-third of the time. The all-fold rate is about:
t5-multiway-frequency-q6.explanation: All-fold rate = (1/3)² = 1/9 ≈ 11.1%. Each extra defender multiplies another 1/3, cutting bluff success exponentially.

t5-multiway-frequency-q7.question: With a half-pot bet, alpha=1/3 and two defenders, each defender's minimum frequency after splitting responsibility is about:
t5-multiway-frequency-q7.explanation: d = 1 − alpha^(1/n) = 1 − (1/3)^(1/2) ≈ 42.3%. Dividing MDF by player count gives 33.4%, a systematic under-defense.

t5-multiway-frequency-q8.question: Can a larger sizing rescue a bluff into a multiway pot?
options: Yes, because the pot is bigger
No, all-fold rate multiplies down and EV gets worse
t5-multiway-frequency-q8.explanation: The all-fold rate is a product across defenders; a larger size raises the fold rate each defender must supply but still crosses several checkpoints. A pot-size bluff into two players is EV −50, worse than half pot.
